newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Chernobyl reactor shut down, no radiation rise.
newsitem.headline: Chernobyl reactor shut down, no radiation rise.

text.p: The Chernobyl nuclear plant shut down automatically on Sunday after the transformer which passes on its energy to Ukraine's power grid developed a defect but radiation levels did not rise, nuclear officials said on Monday.
"It was like applying the brakes on a car. The brakes worked very well," Sergei Parashin, head of the plant about 150 km (80 miles) north of Kiev, told Reuters by telephone.

An automatic message playing at the plant's public affairs office said Reactor no. 3, the only one of four at the plant still working, had been halted and put on a "cooling regime." All equipment had worked normally and safety standards were not breached.
"Radiation levels at the station and around the reactor did not change," the message said.
Chernobyl's fourth reactor exploded in 1986, sending a plume of radioactivity across much of Europe, but about 5,000 people still work there.
The second reactor was stopped after a fire in 1992 and the first one was closed last year in line with plans to cease all operations at the scene of the world's worst civil disaster.
Ukraine, which inherited Chernobyl when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991, has promised to close the plant by 2000 in return for $3.1 billion in Western aid and credits.

"Every crisis should be judged by its consequences. This case confirms the station works safely and the equipment works faultlessly," said Valery Idelson, the plant's chief spokesman, who is based in Kiev.
"No one judges other nuclear plants like they do Chernobyl. We have a psychological effect where Chernobyl is considered a nuclear evil," he added.

Idelson explained that the problem had occurred 600 metres (yards) from the reactor at the transformer, which carries out the final stage of the electricity generating process by passing on energy to Ukraine's power grid.
Failure at any stage of the process leads to an automatic shutdown of the reactor if the system works, Parashin said.
"The only thing is we will suffer economic losses. The station will be shut down for three or four days," he added.
Workers at the plant face an uncertain future ahead of the plant's expected shutdown of the final reactor before the year 2000.

Salaries at Chernobyl are more or less in line with the average in the country's nuclear sector, about 430 hryvnias ($233) a month, Sergei Pavlovsky, head of Chernobyl's international relations department, said recently.
But the workers have not been paid in full or on time for about six months as, like the rest of the energy sector, the plant has lost revenue due to customers not paying their bills.
"We understand there are people worse off," Pavlovsky said. The official average wage among Ukraine's population of 51 million is less than $100 a month.
